passage: In the district cooperative office, Nandini was collecting tea cups when she saw Samir stamping loan forms that had no signature on the last page. "Sir said to push them through today," Samir muttered without looking up. The clerk at the next desk, Ravi, kept typing, and the peon shuffled out. Nandini put the cups down. She did not say "you are wrong". She said, "Samir, is this okay?" The stamp stopped in the air. "I thought..." Samir began, and then, "I will check with Sir." Samir set the pile aside and, for the first time that afternoon, looked at her.

qa.q: What was missing from the loan forms Samir was stamping?
qa.a: The loan forms had no signature on the last page.

qa.q: What might Samir be feeling when the stamp stops in the air after Nandini's question?
qa.a: Samir may feel caught off guard and a little uneasy, but also relieved to be given room to pause; there is no sign of being accused.

qa.q: Why did Nandini's way of asking work, and what else could she add?
qa.a: A plain question left Samir room to think instead of defend, and Nandini could also offer to go with Samir to check with Sir.

qa.q: Why might Ravi have kept typing while Samir stamped?
qa.a: Ravi may have noticed but not felt it was the place, or assumed someone else would say something; staying busy is an easy way to avoid the question.

grounding: A person sees a peer quietly doing something dubious on instruction and asks a plain question, giving space to pause without accusation.

passage: At a Rotterdam warehouse loading bay, Kofi noticed Gabriel peeling expiry labels off pallets of yoghurt and sticking on new ones. Anke, the supervisor, had just walked past saying, "Make it ready for the morning trucks." Two forklift drivers pretended not to see. Kofi walked over with two coffees and said, "Hey, is this okay?" Gabriel froze, holding a label. "Anke said..." "I know. I just wondered." After a moment Gabriel put the label down. "Maybe I should ask her properly." Kofi handed over a coffee and said he would come along.

qa.q: What was Gabriel doing to the pallets of yoghurt?
qa.a: Gabriel was peeling expiry labels off the pallets and sticking on new ones.

qa.q: What might Gabriel be feeling when freezing with a label in hand?
qa.a: Gabriel may feel startled and worried, caught between following Anke's words and a doubt that the job is right.

qa.q: What did Kofi do that gave Gabriel space to stop?
qa.a: Kofi brought coffee, asked a plain "is this okay?" without accusing, and offered to go along, so Gabriel could pause without being blamed.

qa.q: Why might the two forklift drivers have pretended not to see?
qa.a: They may have felt it was not their job or feared trouble with Anke, so ignoring it was the easier way to avoid deciding.

grounding: A person sees a peer doing something dubious on instruction, and a plain question lets the person pause without being accused.

passage:
At the hospital billing counter, the evening queue was long. Suraj noticed Anirban at the next computer adding a line to a patient's bill: a scan the patient never had.
The supervisor had walked past a minute before and said something low to Anirban. The patient, an elderly man with a cloth bag, was counting notes.
Suraj waited until the man had gone to the cashier's window. Then he leaned over. “Hey, just asking. Is this okay?”
Anirban's hands stopped. “Sir said add the package charge to everyone this week.”
“Did he have the scan?”
Anirban stared at the screen for a long moment. Then he opened the bill again and deleted the line. “I'll ask sir to put it in writing,” he said quietly.

qa.q: What did Anirban add to the patient's bill?
qa.a: He added a scan the patient never had.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he leaned over?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about the bill and careful not to accuse, so he chose a plain question.

qa.q: Why was Suraj's question "Is this okay?" a good choice?
qa.a: It let Anirban pause and think without feeling attacked, and he fixed the bill himself.

qa.q: How might the elderly man be affected if nobody had asked?
qa.a: He would have paid for a scan he never had, which could hurt someone counting notes from a cloth bag.

grounding: A colleague sees a peer quietly adding a dubious charge on instruction and asks a plain question that gives him space to pause.

passage:
Hi Dolma,
I hope this doesn't come across wrong. I'm writing because I'd rather ask than wonder.
Yesterday, after the team meeting, I saw you deleting a batch of customer complaints from the tracker. Rajiv and Anand were at their desks too, and I think they noticed as well. I remember Mr Kapoor saying the quarterly numbers “need to look cleaner”.
I'm not accusing you of anything. I know how hard it is when a manager asks for something. I'd probably have done the same. I just want to ask plainly: is this okay? Did he mean delete, or close properly?
If you want to talk, I'll be at the tea counter at four.
Vijay

qa.q: Where does Vijay say he'll be at four?
qa.a: Vijay will be at the tea counter at four.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling as he wrote the email?
qa.a: Vijay felt worried and a little nervous about offending Dolma, which is why the email says it isn't an accusation.

qa.q: What makes Vijay's email a helpful way to raise a concern?
qa.a: It asks a plain question, admits Vijay might have done the same, and offers a private chat, so Dolma can pause without feeling judged.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel reading the email?
qa.a: Dolma might feel caught at first, then relieved that someone noticed and offered a chance to talk it through.

grounding: A colleague notices a peer deleting complaints on instruction and writes a plain, non-accusing question that leaves room to pause.

passage:
You asked about that time at the factory? Okay. I'm Chaitanya, and I was a line supervisor then.
Ruchir, from payroll, sat next to me. One Friday I saw him changing the contract workers' overtime sheets, cutting everyone's hours by two. Manager's orders, the whole payroll room knew. Nobody said a word. The workers were outside at the gate, waiting for their slips.
I didn't want to make a scene. So I just leaned over and asked, “Ruchir, is this okay?”
He went red. “Sir told me.”
“I know. I'm only asking.”
He sat there for maybe a minute. Then he said, “It's not, is it.” He saved the original sheets, and on Monday we both walked into HR together. It started with one small question.

qa.q: By how many hours were the workers' overtime cut?
qa.a: Everyone's hours were cut by two.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel when he asked Ruchir the question?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt uneasy about the change but careful and calm, not wanting to make a scene or accuse Ruchir.

qa.q: What followed from Chaitanya's question, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ruchir saved the original sheets and they went to HR together, because the question let him decide for himself rather than defend himself.

qa.q: How might the contract workers at the gate be affected?
qa.a: They would have lost pay for hours they really worked, so the question protected people who had no voice in that room.

grounding: A colleague sees a peer quietly altering records on a manager's instruction and asks a plain question that lets him pause without being accused.

passage:
I'm Noor, and I sit across from Sarita on the support team.
Last Tuesday, after Mr Bose's quick huddle, I saw her open the complaints sheet and delete rows one by one, the ones marked "refund pending". Kabir, beside her, had his headphones on. Ria watched for a second and looked away. Sarita didn't speak to anyone. She kept rubbing her forehead. I don't know what was going on in her head.
At tea, I didn't accuse her. I just asked, "Sarita, those refund rows. Is this okay?"
She was quiet for a long time. "Mr Bose said the numbers look bad before the review."
"That's what he said," I said. "Is it okay?"
She went back to her desk and pressed undo until the rows came back. That afternoon she emailed Mr Bose asking whether he wanted the rows archived instead, and copied the quality lead.

qa.q: Which rows did Sarita delete from the complaints sheet?
qa.a: The rows marked "refund pending".

qa.q: What might Noor have been feeling while watching Sarita delete the rows?
qa.a: Noor was probably uneasy and concerned, which is why Noor asked a plain question at tea instead of staying silent or accusing Sarita.

qa.q: Why was Noor's plain question more useful than an accusation?
qa.a: It gave Sarita space to stop and think without getting defensive, and let her choose to undo it herself.

qa.q: How might Sarita have experienced Noor's question?
qa.a: Sarita likely felt caught between Mr Bose's instruction and her own doubt, and the gentle question gave her permission to pause.

grounding: Shows a colleague who sees a peer quietly doing something dubious on a manager's instruction and asks a simple question that lets her pause.
